topic: PySpark (optional: Databricks- or Palantir-style roles only)
why: At Databricks and Palantir the FDE works inside the customer's lakehouse: their logs, transactions and eval sets already sit in Delta tables or Foundry datasets at hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes, and the fastest path to a demo on real data is a PySpark transform that runs where their pipelines run, under their cluster's memory limits and their security team's eyes. The differentiator in those loops is not API trivia but being able to look at a stage that has run for forty minutes and say 'one tenant is 40 percent of the rows, that task is the skew, here is the salt' instead of 'Spark is slow', which requires the driver/executor model and the physical plan to be in your head. This topic is optional: if your target list is API-company FDE roles only, topic 36 (DuckDB and dbt) covers the analytics you need and this six hours is better spent on topic 43.
prerequisites: SQL at the level of topic 29 (PostgreSQL): GROUP BY semantics, window functions with frames, join types, null behaviour in aggregates and joins; you will rewrite an existing SQL aggregation and validate the PySpark output against it row for row

Topic 36 (dbt, DuckDB, dimensional modelling): what Parquet is, why data is partitioned by date, and how to export DefenderMate's `llm_calls`, `messages` and `tenants` tables from Postgres to partitioned Parquet with DuckDB `COPY ... TO ... (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (dt))`
Python packaging from topic 25 (`pyproject.toml`, wheels, virtualenvs), because getting your code onto every executor is a packaging problem, not a Spark problem

A laptop with Java 17 installed and `JAVA_HOME` set (`java -version` prints 17 or 21), 8 GB or more of free RAM, and Docker from topic 5 in case you want an isolated `spark` image; `pip install pyspark` does not install a JVM
Enough JVM vocabulary to read an executor log: heap, off-heap, garbage collection pause, `OutOfMemoryError`, what exit code 137 means in a container (topic 5, topic 8)
S3 semantics from topic 14: object listing cost, eventual visibility of partial writes, and the absence of atomic directory rename, which drives the output-commit section of this topic

subtopics.name: When Spark is the right tool, and the driver, executor and cluster-manager model
subtopics.learn: Spark is a driver process (your Python script plus a JVM it controls through Py4J) that turns DataFrame code into a DAG, and a set of executor JVMs that each run `spark.executor.cores` tasks at a time, one task per partition, with a cluster manager (standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or the one Databricks and Foundry hide from you) handing out the containers. In `local[*]` the driver and a single executor share one JVM with one thread per core, which is why a job that works on your laptop fails the first time data must cross a network or exceed one container's memory. Deploy mode `client` runs the driver where you typed `spark-submit` (a notebook kernel, a laptop, a CI runner that gets killed at the 60 minute mark); `cluster` runs it on the cluster, and standalone mode does not support cluster mode for Python applications at all. Before any of this, apply the test from topic 36: if the customer's dataset fits in RAM plus local SSD on one large box (tens to a few hundred gigabytes), DuckDB or Polars will finish before a Spark cluster has started; Spark is justified when data is larger than one node or when the customer already lives in Databricks, EMR or Foundry and your job must run where theirs do.

subtopics.name: Local install, SparkSession.builder and the spark-submit flags that matter
subtopics.learn: `pip install pyspark` ships the Spark jars but not a JVM; Spark 4.x needs Java 17 or 21 (3.5 accepts 8, 11 or 17), and a missing `JAVA_HOME` surfaces as a Py4J gateway error rather than a clear message. Build one session: `SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]").appName("usage").config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8").config("spark.driver.memory", "4g").getOrCreate()`, knowing `spark.driver.memory` cannot change after the JVM is up, so in a notebook it is silently ignored unless the kernel was started with it. Learn the submit line you will type on a customer's edge node: `spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=400 --py-files src.zip --packages io.delta:delta-spark_2.13:4.0.0 --archives venv.tar.gz#env job.py --input s3://... --output s3://... --run-date 2026-09-01`. `--packages` resolves Maven coordinates on the driver and ships the jars (the Delta coordinate must match the Spark and Scala versions exactly), `--py-files` adds `.py`, `.zip` and `.egg` to every executor's `sys.path`, `--files` distributes side files, and `PYSPARK_PYTHON` / `spark.pyspark.python` pins the executor interpreter so you never see `Python in worker has different version than that in driver`. The Web UI is on port 4040 (4041 if taken) for the life of the driver only.

subtopics.name: Lazy evaluation: transformations, actions, jobs, stages, tasks and the shuffle boundary
subtopics.learn: Transformations (`select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, `groupBy().agg`, `join`) only extend a logical plan; nothing executes until an action (`count`, `collect`, `show`, `take`, `first`, `write`, `foreach`) submits a job, so a bug in a `filter` raises at the `show()` ten lines later, and a DataFrame consumed by two actions is recomputed twice unless persisted. Each job is cut into stages at wide dependencies, meaning anything that regroups rows by key (`groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, `repartition`, `orderBy`, a window with `partitionBy`); the rows between stages are written to local disk as shuffle files and fetched over the network by the next stage; a stage is a set of tasks with exactly one task per partition, and a task is the unit that runs on one executor core. Narrow transformations (`select`, `filter`, `union`, `coalesce`) stay inside a stage and are pipelined row by row. Inspect partition counts with `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()`: input partitions come from splitting files at `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (128 MB), post-shuffle partitions from `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200). The drill: read a job, write down how many jobs and stages it will produce and where each shuffle is, then run it and check the Jobs tab; if the prediction is wrong you do not yet understand the cost of the code.

subtopics.name: Reading CSV, JSON and Parquet: explicit schemas, malformed-record policy, partition discovery
subtopics.learn: `spark.read.option("header", True).option("inferSchema", True).csv(path)` performs a full extra pass over the data to guess types and will guess differently tomorrow when one row changes; on any real export pass a schema (a `StructType` or the DDL string `"tenant_id STRING, ts TIMESTAMP, input_tokens BIGINT"`) and choose `mode`: `PERMISSIVE` (default; bad rows become nulls plus a `_corrupt_record` column you must explicitly select to keep, named by `spark.sql.columnNameOfCorruptRecord`), `DROPMALFORMED`, or `FAILFAST` for anything feeding billing. Know that `enforceSchema` defaults to true, so header names are ignored and columns are matched by position, and learn `multiLine`, `escape`, `nullValue`, `timestampFormat` and `dateFormat` (patterns follow Spark's datetime pattern reference, not Java's `SimpleDateFormat`). JSON is line-delimited unless `multiLine=true`; nested fields are addressed as `F.col("usage.output_tokens")`, arrays flattened with `F.explode`, and JSON strings parsed with `F.from_json(col, schema)`. Parquet carries its own schema, is columnar (only selected columns are read), pushes predicates down to row-group statistics, and turns `key=value` directories into partition columns; set `basePath` when reading a subset of partitions so the partition columns survive, and only set `mergeSchema=true` when files genuinely differ because it costs one footer read per file.

subtopics.name: Types, nulls and ANSI mode: the silent-null era versus Spark 4
subtopics.learn: With `spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false` (the Spark 3.x default) an invalid cast, an integer overflow, an out-of-range array index and division by zero all return null, so `CAST(tokens AS INT)` on a bad row quietly shrinks a billing total without any error; Spark 4.0 flips the default to true and those become `CAST_INVALID_INPUT`, `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` and `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` exceptions, which is the first thing that breaks when a customer upgrades their runtime. Reach for `try_cast`, `F.try_divide`, `F.try_add` and `F.try_to_timestamp` where null-on-failure is the intended behaviour, and know the type ladder: `IntegerType` is 32-bit and overflows at 2.1 billion tokens per tenant per period, `DecimalType(18, 6)` for money, `TimestampType` is an instant rendered in the session zone while `TimestampNTZType` (3.4+) is wall-clock time, and `spark.sql.session.timeZone` decides how `F.date_trunc("day", ts)` buckets rows, so set it to `UTC` in code or daily totals differ between your laptop and the cluster. Nulls are skipped by `sum`, `avg` and `count(col)` but counted by `count("*")`, never equal in joins (every null key drops out, or with `eqNullSafe` hashes to one partition), and `F.when(...)` without `.otherwise(...)` yields null.

subtopics.name: Rewriting the SQL aggregation in the DataFrame API: groupBy, agg, pivot, exact versus approximate distincts
subtopics.learn: Take DefenderMate's usage query (per tenant per day: calls, input and output tokens, cost, distinct users, p95 latency) and write it twice: as `spark.sql()` over `df.createOrReplaceTempView("llm_calls")`, and as `df.groupBy("tenant_id", F.date_trunc("day", "ts").alias("day")).agg(F.count("*").alias("calls"), F.sum("input_tokens").alias("input_tokens"), F.sum(F.col("output_tokens") * F.col("price_per_token")).alias("cost"), F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("users"), F.percentile_approx("latency_ms", 0.95, 10000).alias("p95_ms"))`, then prove with `explain()` that both compile to the same physical plan, because they do. Know the traps: `F.countDistinct` over several columns forces an `Expand` operator that multiplies the row count, so use `F.approx_count_distinct(col, rsd=0.01)` (HyperLogLog++) for dashboards and exact counts only where money depends on them; `F.collect_list` and `F.first` have no defined order without a window; `pivot("model", values=[...])` with explicit values avoids an extra distinct job; `rollup` and `cube` emit grouping-set rows with nulls you must label using `F.grouping_id`. Conditions use `&`, `|` and `~` with parentheses, never Python `and`/`or`; `F.expr("...")` is fine when a SQL fragment is clearer. Alias every aggregate so the output schema is stable for tests and downstream readers.

subtopics.name: Window functions: dedup-to-latest, lag-based sessionisation, frame semantics, the single-partition trap
subtopics.learn: `w = Window.partitionBy("tenant_id", "conversation_id").orderBy(F.col("ts").desc())` then `F.row_number().over(w)` and `.filter("rn = 1")` is the canonical dedup-to-latest; `F.lag("ts", 1).over(w)` compared against a gap threshold, followed by a cumulative `F.sum("is_new_session").over(w.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))`, gives session ids with no UDF. Learn the frame rules that differ from intuition: with `orderBy` and no explicit frame the default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, so tied rows share a running total; `rangeBetween` requires a single numeric or date ordering column while `rowsBetween` counts rows; without `orderBy` the frame is the whole partition, which is exactly what `F.max("ts").over(Window.partitionBy("tenant_id"))` wants. A window with no `partitionBy` logs `WARN WindowExec: No Partition Defined for Window operation!` and moves every row to a single task, the number one cause of a stage that never finishes on a customer cluster. Every window costs a shuffle plus a sort, but consecutive windows over identical partition and order keys share one Exchange, so define `w` once and reuse it. Run the same dedup and sessionisation as Postgres window queries (topic 29) on the same export and diff the results.

subtopics.name: Joins: broadcast versus sort-merge, shuffle partitions, AQE, and salting a skewed key
subtopics.learn: For an equi-join Spark chooses BroadcastHashJoin when one side's estimated size is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB; `-1` disables) and otherwise SortMergeJoin, which shuffles both sides on the key into `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200) partitions and sorts each; a non-equi join falls to BroadcastNestedLoopJoin or a Cartesian product that will not finish. Force a small dimension with `F.broadcast(tenants)` or `df.hint("broadcast")` (`MERGE` and `SHUFFLE_HASH` hints also exist), remembering the broadcast side is collected to the driver first, so a 2 GB 'small' table kills the driver, and `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` (300 s) fires when the build side is slow. Adaptive Query Execution (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, on by default since 3.2) uses real shuffle statistics to coalesce the 200 partitions towards `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes` (64 MB), to swap a planned SMJ for a broadcast when a side turns out small, and to split skewed join partitions when `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` sees one larger than `skewedPartitionFactor` (5) times the median and above `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (256 MB). AQE does nothing for skew in a `groupBy`: for a tenant holding 40 percent of rows, salt with `F.concat(F.col("tenant_id"), F.lit("_"), (F.rand() * 16).cast("int"))`, aggregate, strip the salt, aggregate again. Join with `on=["tenant_id"]` (string form) so the key appears once and downstream selects avoid `AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE`, and filter nulls out of join keys because every null hashes to the same partition.

resource.label: Spark SQL guide: Performance Tuning (joins, AQE, broadcast hints)

subtopics.name: Reading the physical plan: Exchange, partial/final HashAggregate, FileScan pushdown, codegen breaks
subtopics.learn: Run `df.explain(mode="formatted")` and read bottom-up. `FileScan parquet [tenant_id#3, tokens#7] Batched: true, PartitionFilters: [(dt#9 = 2026-09-01)], PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(tenant_id)], ReadSchema: struct<...>` tells you column pruning worked, which partitions were skipped, and which predicates reached the Parquet reader; a UDF or a cast wrapped around the column in a filter removes it from `PushedFilters`. `HashAggregate(keys=[tenant_id#3], functions=[partial_sum(tokens#7)])` followed by `Exchange hashpartitioning(tenant_id#3, 200)` and a second `HashAggregate(... functions=[sum(tokens#7)])` is the map-side partial aggregation that makes `groupBy` cheap; `ObjectHashAggregate` shows up for `collect_list`, and `SortAggregate` is the slow fallback. Every `Exchange` is a shuffle and a stage boundary: `hashpartitioning` from groupBy or join, `rangepartitioning` from `orderBy`, `SinglePartition` from a window without `partitionBy` or a `coalesce(1)`, `BroadcastExchange` from a broadcast join. A `*(2)` prefix means WholeStageCodegen stage 2 fused those operators into one generated Java loop; `BatchEvalPython` or `ArrowEvalPython` in the tree marks exactly where a Python UDF broke that fusion. `AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false` means the printed plan is the pre-execution guess; the SQL tab in the UI renders the final plan with real row counts per operator.

subtopics.name: Spark UI and history server: diagnosing skew, spill, small tasks and GC from stage metrics
subtopics.learn: Open `http://localhost:4040` while the job runs, or set `spark.eventLog.enabled=true` and `spark.eventLog.dir` and read it afterwards through the history server on port 18080, which is what you will actually have on a customer cluster. Jobs tab: one job per action; click through to stages. Stages tab: 'Summary Metrics for N Completed Tasks' gives min, 25th percentile, median, 75th and max for Duration, GC Time, Input Size, Shuffle Read, Shuffle Write and Spill (Memory and Disk). Read them like vitals: a max duration many times the median with one giant Shuffle Read is key skew; any non-zero Spill means execution memory ran out and sorts or aggregations went to `spark.local.dir`, so add partitions or memory; thousands of tasks lasting tens of milliseconds means partitions too small (raise `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` or coalesce); GC Time above roughly 10 percent of duration means the heap is thrashing. The Executors tab shows per-executor task time and failures but not Python worker memory, which is why container kills look mysterious (next subtopic). The SQL/DataFrame tab renders the final adaptive plan with rows output and spill per operator. For monitoring, `spark.ui.prometheus.enabled=true` exposes executor metrics at `/metrics/executors/prometheus`, and the REST API at `/api/v1/applications/<id>/stages` lets a CI step fail a build whose stages spilled.

resource.label: Spark docs: Web UI (Jobs, Stages, Storage, Executors, SQL tabs)

subtopics.name: Executor and driver memory: unified memory, overhead, Python worker memory, exit 137 versus Java OOM
subtopics.learn: An executor container is `spark.executor.memory` (JVM heap) plus `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` (max(384 MB, `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` 0.10, or 0.40 for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes) covering JVM native memory, shuffle buffers and, unless `spark.executor.pyspark.memory` is set, every Python UDF worker) plus `spark.memory.offHeap.size` when enabled. Inside the heap 300 MB is reserved and `spark.memory.fraction` (0.6) of the rest is unified memory shared between execution (shuffles, sorts, joins, aggregations) and storage (cached blocks), with `spark.memory.storageFraction` (0.5) as the soft floor storage can be evicted down to; the remaining 40 percent is user memory for your own objects and metadata. Learn the three deaths by their signatures: `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` in executor stderr is the heap; `Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits` or a Kubernetes pod exiting 137 with no Java stack trace is the container total, which in PySpark almost always means Python workers, so raise overhead to 20 to 30 percent or bound them with `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`; a driver death traces to `collect()`, `toPandas()`, a broadcast build side or `collect_list` landing on the driver, guarded by `spark.driver.maxResultSize` (1 GB, error text 'Total size of serialized results ... is bigger than spark.driver.maxResultSize'). Start from 4 to 5 cores per executor, partitions of 100 to 200 MB, heap sized for the largest partition times cores, and only then tune.

resource.label: Spark docs: Tuning Spark (memory management, data structures, GC)

subtopics.name: Python UDFs, pandas UDFs and Arrow: what gets serialised and what Catalyst can no longer see
subtopics.learn: A plain `@F.udf(returnType=...)` runs row by row in a forked `pyspark.daemon` worker on each executor with rows pickled across a socket in batches, and Catalyst treats it as a black box: no predicate pushdown through it, no whole-stage codegen, no null short-circuit, and its cost appears as `BatchEvalPython` in the plan. A `pandas_udf` with type hints (`def f(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series`) moves Arrow record batches of `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch` (10,000) rows instead and is routinely 10 to 100 times faster; `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=true` also makes `toPandas()` and `createDataFrame(pdf)` use Arrow. `mapInPandas(func, schema)` hands you an iterator of pandas frames per partition (model scoring), and `groupBy().applyInPandas(func, schema)` hands you one frame per group, which means one skewed tenant's entire group must fit in a single Python worker's memory. Spark 3.5 adds Arrow-optimised regular UDFs (`@udf(useArrow=True)`) and Python UDTFs. The rule before writing any UDF: check `pyspark.sql.functions` and the higher-order array functions (`F.transform`, `F.filter`, `F.aggregate`, `F.exists`) first, because most UDFs in customer code are `to_timestamp`, `regexp_extract`, `from_json` or `split` written by hand. Python exceptions inside a UDF surface as `PythonException` with the Python traceback in the driver output (`spark.sql.execution.pyspark.udf.simplifiedTraceback.enabled`); `print` inside a UDF goes to executor stderr, not to your notebook.

resource.label: PySpark tutorial: Apache Arrow in PySpark (pandas UDFs, mapInPandas, applyInPandas)

subtopics.name: Writing output: partitionBy, file sizing, overwrite semantics, and atomic commits on S3
subtopics.learn: `df.repartition("tenant_id", "dt").write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("tenant_id", "dt").option("compression", "zstd").parquet(out)` yields one file per output directory because the rows for each partition value are colocated in one task; without the `repartition`, every task writes a file into every directory it touches, and 200 tasks times 500 tenants times 30 days is three million small files that make listing slower than reading. `coalesce(n)` merges partitions without a shuffle but also lowers the parallelism of the entire upstream stage, `repartition(n)` shuffles round-robin, `option("maxRecordsPerFile", n)` caps file size; aim for files of 128 MB to 1 GB. Save modes are `append`, `overwrite`, `ignore` and `errorifexists` (default), and `overwrite` with `partitionBy` deletes the whole output path first under the default `spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=static`; set `dynamic` so re-running one `dt` replaces only that partition, which is what makes the job idempotent per run date. On S3 there is no atomic rename, so the Hadoop `FileOutputCommitter` v1 renames every file twice and is slow, v2 (`mapreduce.fileoutputcommitter.algorithm.version=2`) leaves partial output visible on failure, and the correct answer is the S3A committers (`spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.committer.name=magic` with `spark.sql.sources.commitProtocolClass=org.apache.spark.internal.io.cloud.PathOutputCommitProtocol` and `spark.sql.parquet.output.committer.class=org.apache.spark.internal.io.cloud.BindingParquetOutputCommitter`) or a table format such as Delta. Readers gate on the `_SUCCESS` marker or a table commit, never on the presence of files.

resource.label: Spark docs: Integration with Cloud Infrastructures (S3 committers, consistency, rename)

subtopics.name: Delta Lake: transaction log, MERGE for late data, time travel, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, schema enforcement
subtopics.learn: Delta is Parquet plus a `_delta_log/` of JSON commits (with a Parquet checkpoint every 10) giving ACID table-level commits under optimistic concurrency, so a failed job leaves no partial files visible and two writers to the same partition get a `ConcurrentAppendException` instead of corrupt data. Enable it with `pip install delta-spark` and `configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder)`, which sets `spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension` and `spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog=org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog`. Late-arriving DefenderMate events are absorbed with `DeltaTable.forPath(spark, out).alias("t").merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.tenant_id = s.tenant_id AND t.day = s.day").whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()`; dedupe the source first or MERGE fails with 'multiple source rows matched', and put partition predicates in the ON clause so it prunes files. `spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 12).load(out)` and `DESCRIBE HISTORY` let you show a customer exactly what the billing table said last Tuesday. `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (tenant_id)` compacts the small files that MERGE and streaming create; `VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS` deletes unreferenced files and also destroys time travel past that horizon, which is why `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled` refuses shorter windows by default. Schema enforcement rejects a write whose columns differ with an `AnalysisException`; evolve deliberately with `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`, and use `.option("replaceWhere", "day = '2026-09-01'")` for a partition-scoped overwrite. Databricks layers Photon, liquid clustering and deletion vectors on top; the log format is the same one you run locally.

resource.label: Delta Lake docs: Table deletes, updates, and merges (MERGE INTO)

subtopics.name: cache, persist and checkpoint: when materialisation helps and when it removes pushdown
subtopics.learn: `df.cache()` is `persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)` for DataFrames (RDDs default to `MEMORY_ONLY`), is lazy until the next action, and only pays off when the same DataFrame feeds two or more actions, such as a `count()` for a data-quality gate followed by a `write`, or an iterative algorithm; a frame cached and used once just costs memory plus the conversion to columnar blocks. Cache after your filters, not before: reads from a cached relation come from `InMemoryTableScan`, so predicates no longer reach the Parquet scan and partition pruning is gone for every downstream query. Watch the Storage tab for 'Fraction Cached' below 100 percent, meaning blocks were evicted because execution memory reclaimed the space and recomputation is happening anyway; call `unpersist()` when finished or `spark.catalog.clearCache()`. `checkpoint()` (after `sc.setCheckpointDir`) writes the data to reliable storage and truncates lineage, which is the fix when a plan is so deep that Catalyst analysis itself takes minutes or a `StackOverflowError` appears on the driver, typically in loops that keep re-assigning `df = df.join(...)`; `localCheckpoint()` does the same to executor disk without durability. Never `cache()` to make a one-shot job faster; fix the plan.

resource.label: PySpark API reference: DataFrame.persist and StorageLevel

subtopics.name: Testing and packaging a job that runs identically on a laptop and on the customer's cluster
subtopics.learn: Structure the job as pure functions, `def daily_usage(llm_calls: DataFrame, tenants: DataFrame) -> DataFrame`, with a thin `main()` that parses `--input`, `--output` and `--run-date` and builds the session, so tests call the functions on `spark.createDataFrame([...], schema)` using a session fixture built with `master("local[2]")`, `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2` and `spark.ui.enabled=false` (session-scoped, since JVM startup costs seconds). Assert with `pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected, checkRowOrder=False)` and `assertSchemaEqual`, and include one test that runs the reference Postgres SQL against exported fixtures and compares row for row; that is the test that catches time zone and null-handling drift. Packaging is where laptop-green jobs die on clusters: any module imported inside a UDF or transform must exist on every executor, so ship it with `--py-files src.zip` (pure Python) or build the environment with `venv-pack -o venv.tar.gz` and submit `--archives venv.tar.gz#env --conf spark.pyspark.python=./env/bin/python` (or `conda-pack`, or a Docker image on Kubernetes); `ModuleNotFoundError` thrown from inside `BatchEvalPython` is this bug every single time. Pin `pyspark` to the cluster's exact minor version in `pyproject.toml`, set `spark.sql.session.timeZone=UTC` in code rather than trusting the cluster, and log from the driver's Python logger only, because executor stderr is not yours to read on a customer's platform.

resource.label: PySpark tutorial: Python Package Management (py-files, archives, venv-pack, conda-pack)

subtopics.name: Where PySpark lives in Databricks and Foundry, and what Spark Connect changes
subtopics.learn: On Databricks `spark` is pre-created in every notebook, production work runs as Jobs on job clusters (ephemeral, cheaper) rather than all-purpose clusters, tables live in Unity Catalog as `catalog.schema.table` and are Delta by default, Photon swaps the execution engine underneath without code changes, and Databricks Connect runs your local IDE's PySpark against a remote cluster because it is built on Spark Connect. In Palantir Foundry the unit is a dataset (a versioned, branchable Parquet or Delta directory) and the code is a transform: `@transform_df(Output("/Org/usage/daily"), calls=Input("/Org/raw/llm_calls"))` returning a DataFrame, built by Foundry's scheduler with lineage recorded, while `@incremental()` transforms read only `.dataframe("added")` rows since the previous build, which is how a Palantir FDE ships a daily pipeline in an afternoon. Spark Connect (3.4+, `SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002")`, the `pyspark-client` package in 4.0) replaces the in-process Py4J driver with a thin gRPC client: the DataFrame API is unchanged, but `sparkContext`, RDDs and `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` are gone, and a client crash no longer kills the driver. Know these three well enough that a customer conversation about 'our pipelines' goes straight to their transform code.

resource.label: Palantir Foundry docs: Python transforms overview

outcomes: You can rewrite DefenderMate's per-tenant, per-day usage aggregation (calls, tokens, cost, distinct users, p95 latency) as a PySpark job, run it with `spark-submit --master local[4]` over Parquet exports, and show with `assertDataFrameEqual` that it matches the Postgres query row for row, including on days with nulls and time zone edges.

You can draw the driver, executor and cluster-manager diagram from memory, place the Python process, the JVM, Py4J and the Python UDF workers on it, and state which process dies and with what error for `collect()`, an oversized broadcast, an `applyInPandas` group, and a large shuffle.

You can read `explain(mode="formatted")` for an unfamiliar job and identify every Exchange and its cause, the join strategy chosen, whether filters reached the Parquet scan, and where a Python UDF broke codegen, and predict the number of stages before running it.

You can open the Spark UI on a slow stage and within five minutes distinguish key skew, spill, too many small tasks and GC pressure from the stage summary metrics, naming the code or config change for each.

You can choose between broadcast and sort-merge joins from table sizes, set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` and AQE deliberately, salt a skewed `groupBy` key, and demonstrate the stage time before and after on a synthetically skewed tenant.

You can write partitioned Parquet or Delta output that is idempotent per run date (dynamic partition overwrite or MERGE), produces files between 128 MB and 1 GB rather than thousands of small ones, and commits atomically on S3 with a committer you can name.

You can package the job so it runs unchanged on a laptop and on a customer's YARN or Kubernetes cluster (pure-function transforms, pytest with a local session, `--archives` venv, pinned pyspark), and explain each `spark-submit` flag you used.

You can tell a customer in one minute whether Spark is the right tool for their 50 GB or 5 TB, and if they are on Databricks or Foundry, describe where your transform would live and how it would be scheduled.
failureModes: `inferSchema=true` on a nightly CSV export doubles the read and infers `tenant_id` as long on Monday and string on Tuesday when one UUID appears; the downstream join silently drops every row and the dashboard shows zero usage before anyone notices the schema flip.

`df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("dt").parquet(path)` under the default `partitionOverwriteMode=static` deletes two years of history in the customer's bucket during a one-day backfill, and the only copy was the output of the job that deleted it.

A Python UDF parses timestamps over two billion rows: thirty times slower than `F.to_timestamp`, predicate pushdown gone, and the `pyspark.daemon` workers push each Kubernetes pod over its limit, so executors die with exit code 137 and no `OutOfMemoryError` anywhere in the logs.

One tenant holds 40 percent of rows; `groupBy("tenant_id")` sends all of them to one task that runs three hours while the other 199 finish in seconds, AQE skew handling does not apply because it is an aggregation rather than a join, and the nightly SLA is missed until someone salts the key.

`toPandas()` on a 'small' filtered result that is actually 6 GB kills the driver with `spark.driver.maxResultSize` after two hours of upstream compute; the fix was to write the result to a table and read one partition, and to put a `count()` guard in front of any driver-side collection.

The job passes locally and fails on the cluster with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'defendermate_utils'` inside `BatchEvalPython`, because the package was installed on the edge node only and never shipped with `--py-files` or an `--archives` environment.

`spark.sql.session.timeZone` is the laptop's local zone in development and UTC on the cluster, so `date_trunc("day", ts)` buckets shift by several hours between environments; the PySpark daily totals disagree with the Postgres billing query and the discrepancy is blamed on Spark for a week.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what happens, process by process, when this line runs: `df.groupBy("tenant_id").agg(F.sum("tokens")).write.parquet(path)`. How many jobs and stages, where is the shuffle, what does the driver do versus the executors, and what changes if `df` came from a Python UDF?

A customer's nightly PySpark job went from 20 minutes to 3 hours after they onboarded one large new client. The code did not change. Take me through your diagnosis in the Spark UI and the fixes you would try, in order, with the trade-off of each.

Design a pipeline that ingests LLM call logs (JSON, about 2 TB per day, events arriving up to 48 hours late) into a per-tenant daily usage table that finance bills from. Cover idempotent reruns, late data, partitioning and file sizing, and how you validate against the source of truth.
When would you use a pandas UDF versus a plain Python UDF versus a built-in expression? For each, what exactly is serialised, where does it run, and what does Catalyst lose the ability to do?

Executor containers are being killed with exit code 137 but there is no `OutOfMemoryError` in any JVM log. Explain the memory regions involved in a PySpark executor and what you would change, and how you would confirm the fix from the UI or metrics.

Explain sort-merge join versus broadcast hash join: how Spark chooses, what goes wrong when you force a broadcast, how AQE changes the decision at runtime, and why AQE still will not save a skewed groupBy.

A customer with 50 GB of data wants everything on Spark because 'that is what Databricks is for'. Are they right? How would you decide, what would you propose instead if not, and how would you say it to their head of data without losing the room?
proofOfWork: A public repository `defendermate-spark-usage` containing: (1) an exporter that dumps `llm_calls`, `messages` and `tenants` from DefenderMate's Postgres to Parquet partitioned by `dt`; (2) `jobs/usage_daily.py` written as pure-function transforms with an argparse `main()` taking `--input`, `--output` and `--run-date`, writing with dynamic partition overwrite so any day can be rerun; (3) `sql/usage_daily.sql`, the reference query run in Postgres, and a pytest that asserts the PySpark output equals it with `assertDataFrameEqual`; (4) `NOTES.md` holding the annotated `explain(mode="formatted")` output with every Exchange and the join strategy labelled, a before-and-after table of stage summary metrics (median versus max task duration, shuffle read, spill) from salting a synthetically skewed tenant given 40 percent of rows, and a memory table listing the four OOM scenarios you actually triggered (`collect()`, oversized broadcast, `applyInPandas` on the skewed tenant, shuffle spill) with the exact error text and which process died; (5) a Delta variant of the writer that absorbs a replayed batch of late events via MERGE, with the `DESCRIBE HISTORY` output showing the commit and a `versionAsOf` read proving the previous state is recoverable. This is the artefact you open when a Databricks or Palantir interviewer says 'show me Spark you have written'.
